title: The Spelling Bee Champion
summary: A boy who struggles with spelling practices every day with his teacher's encouragement and does his personal best at the school spelling bee.
poll: Winning is the only thing that matters in a competition.

versions.title: The Spelling Bee Champion
versions.text:
Yousef did not like spelling. He got a bad grade on a test.

One day, his teacher, Ms. Huda, said there would be a spelling bee. Yousef felt nervous. He did not want to join.

"Just try your best," she said. "That is what matters." She gave Yousef a list of words. She showed him how to break each word into small parts.

Yousef practiced every day. He wrote the words. He said them out loud. His sister helped him too.

Slowly, Yousef got better. He felt less nervous each day.

On the day of the bee, his heart beat fast. He took a deep breath. He spelled word after word! His class clapped.

Then Yousef missed one hard word. He did not win first place. But he had spelled more words than he thought he could.

Ms. Huda smiled. "You worked so hard," she said. "I am proud of you." Yousef smiled too. He had done his best.

versions.title: The Spelling Bee Champion
versions.text:
Yousef did not like spelling very much. He got a low grade on a test. It made him feel upset.

One day, his teacher, Ms. Huda, said there would be a bee. It was in a few weeks. Yousef felt very nervous. He did not want to join.

"Just try your best," she said. "That is what matters." She gave Yousef a list of words. She showed him how to break each word into small parts, called syllables.

From that day on, Yousef practiced a bit every day. He wrote the words down. He said them out loud. He used flashcards his sister made for him.

Slowly, Yousef got better. Each day, he felt a bit less nervous. He felt more sure of himself too.

On the day of the bee, his heart pounded. He took a deep breath. He spelled word after word! His classmates clapped for him.

Then Yousef missed one hard word. He did not win first place. Still, he had spelled far more words than he thought he could.

"You worked so hard," Ms. Huda said, smiling. "I am proud of you." Yousef smiled too. He knew he had done his best.

versions.title: The Spelling Bee Champion
versions.text:
Yousef had never liked spelling much. He had just gotten a low grade on a test. It left him feeling upset and a little embarrassed.

One day, his teacher, Ms. Huda, said the school would hold a spelling bee. It was in a few weeks. Yousef felt very nervous. At first, he did not want to join.

"Just try your best," Ms. Huda told him. "That is what matters, not winning." She gave Yousef a list of tricky words to practice. She showed him a trick: break each word into small parts, called syllables, to make it easier to remember.

From that day on, Yousef practiced a bit every day. He wrote the words down. He said them out loud again and again. He used flashcards his sister helped him make.

Slowly, Yousef began to improve. With each day, he felt a bit less nervous. He felt more sure of himself too.

On the day of the bee, Yousef's heart pounded as he walked up to the mic. He took a deep breath. He spelled word after word, which surprised even him. His classmates clapped loudly each time.

Then Yousef missed one hard word, and he did not win first place. Even so, he had spelled far more words than he ever thought he could.

"You worked so hard, and it showed today," Ms. Huda said, smiling. Yousef smiled back. Deep down, he knew he had done his best.

versions.title: The Spelling Bee Champion
versions.text:
Yousef had never liked spelling much. He had just gotten a low grade on a test. It left him upset, and more than a little embarrassed in front of his classmates.

One day, Ms. Huda said the school would hold its spelling bee in a few weeks. As soon as he heard the news, Yousef felt a wave of nervousness. At first, he did not even want to sign up.

"Just try your best," Ms. Huda told him, noticing how worried he looked. "That matters here, not winning first place." She gave Yousef a list of tricky words to practice. She also showed him a useful trick: break each long word into small parts, called syllables, which made the words easier to say.

From that day on, Yousef made himself practice a bit every day, without skipping once. He wrote the words down, said them out loud again and again, and used flashcards his sister had helped him make.

Slowly, Yousef began to see real gains. With each day of practice, he felt a bit less nervous. He felt more sure of himself too.

On the day of the bee, Yousef's heart pounded as he walked up to the mic in front of the whole school. He took a deep breath and spelled word after word, which surprised even him. His classmates clapped loudly each time he got one right.

Then Yousef missed one hard word, and he did not win first place. Even so, he had spelled far more words than he had ever thought he could, which felt like its own kind of win.

"You worked so hard, and it showed today," Ms. Huda said, smiling warmly. Yousef smiled back at his teacher. Deep down, he knew he had done his best.

versions.title: The Spelling Bee Champion
versions.text:
Few things feel worse than struggling with something in front of your whole class. That is exactly how Yousef felt about spelling.

Yousef had never been confident about spelling. He had just gotten a low grade on his most recent test. So when Ms. Huda announced the school's spelling bee, Yousef felt a wave of nervousness. At first, he did not even want to sign up.

"Just do your best," Ms. Huda encouraged him gently. "That is what truly matters, not winning." She handed Yousef a list of tricky words. She taught him a useful trick: break each long word into smaller parts, called syllables, to make it easier to say.

Taking her advice to heart, Yousef built a simple daily routine. Every afternoon, he wrote the words down, said them aloud several times, and quizzed himself with flashcards his sister had helped him make. He treated each session like its own small challenge.

Slowly, Yousef's spelling began to improve. With each bit of improvement, his confidence grew a little stronger. By the time the bee arrived, he felt far more ready than he ever thought he would.

On the day of the bee, Yousef's heart pounded as he walked up to the mic in front of the whole school. He took a steady breath and spelled word after word correctly, surprising even himself. His classmates cheered for him each time he got one right.

Eventually, Yousef missed one unusually hard word and did not win first place. Even so, he had spelled far more words correctly than he had ever imagined, and that alone felt like a real win.

"You worked incredibly hard, and it clearly showed today," Ms. Huda told him. Yousef smiled, knowing he had given his very best effort, and that, in the end, was what mattered most.

versions.title: The Spelling Bee Champion
versions.text:

Yousef had never felt confident about spelling, and he had just gotten another low grade on his most recent test. So when Ms. Huda announced the school's spelling bee, a wave of nervousness washed over him. At first, he did not even want to sign up, worried that he would only embarrass himself in front of everyone.

"Just do your best," Ms. Huda encouraged him gently, noticing how worried he looked. "That is what truly matters here, not winning first place." She handed Yousef a list of tricky words and taught him a useful trick: break each long, unfamiliar word into smaller parts, called syllables, which made the words easier to remember and say.

Taking her advice seriously, Yousef built himself a simple daily routine. Every afternoon after his homework, he wrote the words down, said them aloud several times, and quizzed himself with flashcards his sister had helped him make. He treated each session almost like its own small challenge, one word at a time.

Slowly, over the following weeks, Yousef's spelling began to improve, and with every small gain, his confidence grew a little stronger. His parents noticed the change too, and praised him for sticking with something that once felt so frustrating. By the time the bee arrived, Yousef felt far more ready than he ever imagined.

Eventually, Yousef missed one unusually hard word and did not end up winning first place. Even so, he had spelled far more words correctly than he had ever imagined, and that felt like a real win to him.

"You worked incredibly hard this whole time, and it clearly showed today," Ms. Huda told him. Yousef smiled, knowing he had given his very best effort, and in the end, that mattered most of all.

versions.title: The Spelling Bee Champion
versions.text:
Few things feel worse than struggling with something in front of your whole class, and that is exactly how Yousef felt about spelling for most of the school year.

Yousef had never been especially confident about spelling, and he had just received a disappointing grade on his most recent spelling test. So when his teacher, Ms. Huda, announced that the school would hold its annual spelling bee in a few weeks, Yousef felt a sudden wave of nervousness. At first, he did not even want to sign up, worried that he might embarrass himself in front of everyone.

"Just do your best," Ms. Huda encouraged him gently, noticing how worried he looked. "That is what truly matters, not winning first place." She handed Yousef a list of especially tricky words and taught him a useful trick: breaking each long word into smaller parts, called syllables, which made unfamiliar words considerably easier to remember and pronounce.

Taking her advice to heart, Yousef built a simple daily routine for himself. Every afternoon, he wrote the words down, said them aloud several times, and quizzed himself using flashcards his older sister had helped him make. He treated each practice session almost like its own small challenge to work through, one careful step at a time.

Slowly but surely, Yousef's spelling began to improve, and with every bit of improvement, his confidence grew a little stronger. His parents noticed the change too, and they praised him for sticking with something that had once felt so frustrating. By the time the spelling bee finally arrived, Yousef felt far more prepared than he ever thought he would.

On the day of the competition, Yousef's heart pounded as he walked up to the microphone in front of the entire school. He took a steady breath and spelled word after word correctly, surprising even himself. His classmates cheered for him every time he succeeded.

Eventually, Yousef missed one unusually difficult word and did not win first place. Even so, he had spelled far more words correctly than he had ever imagined possible, and that alone felt like a real accomplishment.

"You worked incredibly hard, and it clearly showed today," Ms. Huda told him afterward, smiling warmly. Yousef smiled back, knowing that he had truly given his very best effort.

Later that evening, Yousef's older sister reminded him that even the students who had won the spelling bee had once struggled with spelling too, just like he had. What mattered most, she explained, was that he had kept practicing even when it felt difficult, and that same kind of effort would help him with far more than just spelling words.

versions.title: The Spelling Bee Champion
versions.text:
Few experiences feel more uncomfortable than struggling with something publicly, in front of an entire classroom, and that discomfort described precisely how Yousef felt whenever spelling tests were returned to students.

Yousef had never felt particularly confident about spelling, and he had just received yet another disappointing grade on his most recent test. So when his teacher, Ms. Huda, announced that the school would hold its annual spelling bee in a few weeks, a wave of nervousness washed over him immediately. At first, he did not even want to participate, worried that he would only embarrass himself in front of his classmates.

"Just do your best," Ms. Huda encouraged him gently, noticing how anxious he appeared. "That is what truly matters here, not necessarily winning." She handed Yousef a list of especially tricky words and taught him a valuable technique: dividing each long, unfamiliar word into smaller syllables, which made the words considerably easier to remember and articulate correctly.

Taking her advice seriously, Yousef established a simple daily routine for himself. Every afternoon after completing his homework, he wrote the words down carefully, pronounced them aloud several times, and quizzed himself using flashcards his older sister had patiently helped him create. He approached each practice session almost like an individual challenge worth overcoming, one syllable at a time.

Slowly but surely, over the following weeks, Yousef's spelling noticeably began to improve, and with every incremental achievement, his confidence grew correspondingly stronger. His parents noticed this transformation as well, praising him often for demonstrating such resilience in sticking with something that had once felt genuinely frustrating. By the time the spelling bee finally arrived, Yousef felt considerably more prepared than he ever imagined he would.

On the day of the competition, Yousef's heart pounded nervously as he walked toward the microphone in front of the entire school. He took a steady breath and spelled word after word correctly, surprising even himself with each small success. His classmates cheered enthusiastically for him every single time he succeeded.

Eventually, Yousef missed one unusually difficult word and did not ultimately win first place. Even so, he had spelled far more words correctly than he had ever imagined possible, and that outcome alone felt like a genuine achievement to him.

"You demonstrated real perseverance this entire time, and it clearly showed today," Ms. Huda told him afterward, smiling warmly. Yousef smiled back, understanding deep down that he had truly given his very best effort, and in the end, that mattered more than any trophy could.

Later that evening, Yousef's older sister reminded him that even the students who had ultimately won the spelling bee had once struggled with spelling themselves, just as he had. What mattered most, she explained, was that he had kept practicing even when progress felt slow and difficult, since that same resilience would serve him well in challenges far beyond spelling words.

keyWords.definition: to say or write the letters of a word in the correct order
keyWords.example: Can you spell your name for me?

keyWords.definition: to do something again and again in order to get better at it
keyWords.example: She practices the piano every afternoon.

keyWords.definition: feeling worried or afraid about something that is about to happen
keyWords.example: I felt nervous before my first day at a new school.

keyWords.definition: a group of letters or sounds that has a meaning
keyWords.example: Can you find that word in the dictionary?

keyWords.definition: a person whose job is to help students learn
keyWords.example: Our teacher read us a story after lunch.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A boy who struggles with spelling, practices daily, and does his best at the bee
A boy who wins a big soccer trophy for his entire school team last spring
A girl who teaches her whole class how to spell new words correctly in school
A boy who forgets about the spelling bee this year and goes home
questions.why: The story follows Yousef as he practices spelling every day and does his personal best at the spelling bee.

wrong.B: The story is not about a soccer trophy.
wrong.C: A girl teaching the class is not part of the story.
wrong.D: Yousef remembers and prepares for the spelling bee; he does not forget it.

Yousef missed a hard word at the bee
questions.why: Right after hearing about the spelling bee, Yousef felt nervous and at first did not want to sign up.

wrong.A: Winning happens, if at all, only after practice and the competition, not right after the announcement.
wrong.C: The flashcards were made after Yousef began practicing, not right after the announcement.
wrong.D: Missing a word happens on the day of the bee, much later in the story.

questions.stem: Why did Yousef's spelling slowly improve?
options: His sister spelled the words for him during the bee, whispering each letter
The words in the bee were much easier than his tests at school
He practiced a little every day using flashcards and syllables
Ms. Huda gave him the answers ahead of time, in a secret note
questions.why: Yousef practiced daily, breaking words into syllables and using flashcards, which helped his spelling improve.

wrong.A: Yousef spelled the words himself during the bee.
wrong.B: The story does not say the bee's words were easier than his tests.
wrong.D: Ms. Huda taught him a technique; she did not give him the answers.

questions.stem: Who helped Yousef make flashcards to practice with?
options: Ms. Huda
A judge at the spelling bee
His classmate
His older sister
questions.why: Yousef's older sister helped him make the flashcards he used to practice.

wrong.A: Ms. Huda gave Yousef the word list and the syllable trick, not the flashcards.
wrong.B: There is no mention of a judge helping Yousef practice.
wrong.C: A classmate is not mentioned helping Yousef practice.

questions.stem: Why did Yousef feel nervous when he first heard about the spelling bee?
options: He did not feel confident about spelling and was afraid of doing poorly in front of others
He did not like his teacher, Ms. Huda, and wanted to leave the classroom early
He wanted to skip school that day, so he pretended to be sick and stayed in bed
He had never heard of a spelling bee before and did not know what it was or how it works
questions.why: Since Yousef had just gotten a low grade on a spelling test, he worried about doing poorly in front of his classmates.

wrong.B: Yousef's nervousness was not about disliking his teacher.
wrong.C: There is no mention of Yousef wanting to skip school.
wrong.D: His nervousness came from his struggles with spelling, not from unfamiliarity with the event.

questions.stem: In the story, the word nervous means —
options: Excited and very happy about something fun that is going to happen
Worried or afraid about something that is about to happen
Feeling very angry at a close, good friend of yours
Feeling quite tired after a very long day of work
questions.why: Yousef felt nervous, or worried, about joining the spelling bee because he was not confident in his spelling.

wrong.A: Nervous does not mean excited and happy.
wrong.C: Yousef was not angry at a friend in the story.
wrong.D: Nervous is different from feeling tired.

questions.stem: How did Yousef feel at the start of the story compared to after he practiced for weeks?
options: Confident at first, then nervous later on in the contest
Angry at first, then happy later when he won a prize
Nervous and unsure at first, then more confident later
Bored at first, then excited later about the competition
questions.why: Yousef began the story feeling nervous and unsure, but weeks of practice made him feel more confident by the time of the bee.

wrong.A: Yousef was nervous at first, not confident; his confidence grew later.
wrong.B: Yousef was not angry at the start of the story.
wrong.D: Yousef was nervous, not bored, at the start.

questions.stem: Why did the author include the part where Yousef misses a hard word and does not win first place?
options: To show that Yousef did not practice nearly enough for the contest
To make the whole story funny and a bit silly for readers
To explain all the official rules of a spelling bee at school
To show that doing your personal best matters more than winning
questions.why: Even though Yousef did not win, the story shows that his effort and improvement were what truly mattered.

wrong.A: The story shows Yousef practiced a great deal, which is why he did so much better than before.
wrong.B: The ending is meant to be meaningful, not funny.
wrong.C: The story does not explain official spelling bee rules.

LOW.prompt: Do you think Yousef should be proud of how he did at the spelling bee, even though he did not win first place? Explain why or why not, using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: Yes, I think Yousef should be proud of himself. In the story, he had gotten a low grade on his spelling test and felt very nervous about the bee. But he practiced every day, and at the bee he spelled many words correctly, even though he missed one hard word near the end.

keyWords.definition: to give someone support or confidence to do something
keyWords.example: My coach encourages me before every game.

keyWords.definition: a feeling of trust in your own ability to do something
keyWords.example: Winning the small race gave her more confidence.

keyWords.definition: to get better at something over time
keyWords.example: His handwriting began to improve after months of practice.

keyWords.definition: a set of actions done regularly, usually in the same order
keyWords.example: Brushing my teeth every morning is part of my routine.

keyWords.definition: something difficult that requires effort to do or solve
keyWords.example: Climbing the tall hill was a real challenge for the younger kids.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of this story?
options: Yousef easily wins the entire spelling bee without any real practice or help
With encouragement, Yousef practices daily and grows more confident, even without winning
Ms. Huda flatly refuses to ever help Yousef improve his spelling at school or at home
Yousef's older sister competes in the spelling bee instead of him this year
questions.why: The story centers on Yousef building a practice routine with his teacher's encouragement and growing more confident, even without winning first place.

wrong.A: Yousef practices a great deal; he does not win easily without effort.
wrong.C: Ms. Huda actively helps Yousef with word lists and a syllable trick.
wrong.D: Yousef, not his sister, competes in the spelling bee.

questions.stem: What trick did Ms. Huda teach Yousef to help him with long, tricky words?
options: Breaking each word into smaller parts called syllables
Memorizing words backward, from last letter to first
Only practicing the easiest words on the list
Skipping words with more than one syllable
questions.why: Ms. Huda taught Yousef to divide long words into syllables, making them easier to remember.

wrong.B: The story does not mention memorizing words backward.
wrong.C: Yousef practiced the tricky words, not just the easiest ones.
wrong.D: Yousef practiced long words rather than skipping them.

questions.stem: What did Yousef's daily practice routine include?
options: Watching videos about spelling bees every night after dinner
Asking his classmates to quiz him at recess each day
Reading the dictionary from start to finish in just one week
Writing words down, saying them aloud, and using flashcards
questions.why: Yousef's routine involved writing the words down, saying them aloud, and quizzing himself with flashcards.

wrong.A: The story does not mention watching videos.
wrong.B: Classmates quizzing him at recess is not described in the story.
wrong.C: Reading the whole dictionary is not part of his routine.

questions.stem: Why did Yousef's confidence grow over the weeks before the bee?
options: Ms. Huda promised he would win
The words on the final list turned out to be very easy
His spelling kept improving the more he practiced
His classmates stopped teasing him about spelling
questions.why: As Yousef practiced more, his spelling improved, and that improvement is what built his confidence.

wrong.A: Ms. Huda encouraged effort, not a guaranteed win.
wrong.B: The bee's words are described as difficult, not easy.
wrong.D: The story does not mention classmates teasing Yousef.

questions.stem: Why do you think Ms. Huda told Yousef that doing his best mattered more than winning?
options: She did not think Yousef could ever improve at spelling
She wanted to encourage him to try without being afraid of failing
She did not care about the spelling bee, and she was bored
She wanted him to quit before the competition began, so he could rest
questions.why: By focusing on effort rather than winning, Ms. Huda helped Yousef feel less afraid of failing and more willing to try.

wrong.A: Ms. Huda's encouragement suggests she believed Yousef could improve.
wrong.C: Ms. Huda clearly cared, since she gave Yousef a word list and a helpful technique.
wrong.D: Ms. Huda encouraged Yousef to participate, not to quit.

questions.stem: In the story, the word challenge means —
options: Something difficult that takes effort to overcome
A prize given to the winner of a contest
A short list of easy words to read aloud in class
A mistake that is made by accident in the morning
questions.why: Yousef treated each practice session as a challenge, something difficult that required effort to work through.

wrong.B: A challenge is not the same as a prize.
wrong.C: The challenging words were described as tricky, not easy.
wrong.D: A challenge is not the same as an accidental mistake.

questions.stem: How does the story mostly organize events?
options: It compares Yousef's spelling skill to his older sister's spelling skill
It lists spelling rules and facts with no real story about Yousef
It describes the spelling bee first, and then goes back in time
It follows time order: the bad grade, the announcement, practice, and the bee
questions.why: The story moves in time order, from Yousef's low grade to the announcement, his practice, and finally the spelling bee.

wrong.A: The story focuses on Yousef's own experience, not a comparison with his sister's spelling.
wrong.B: The story follows Yousef, not a list of spelling rules.
wrong.C: The story begins with the bad grade and announcement, not with the bee.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Yousef's family from how they reacted to his hard work?
options: They were disappointed that he did not win first place at the contest
They thought spelling was not very important
They were proud of his effort and encouraged him along the way
They flatly refused to help him study at home
questions.why: Yousef's parents praised his improvement, and his sister helped him practice, showing they were proud of his effort.

wrong.A: The story shows the family praising his effort, not expressing disappointment.
wrong.B: The family's support suggests they valued spelling and effort.
wrong.D: Yousef's sister actively helped him make flashcards at home.

MID.prompt: Explain how Yousef's daily practice and his teacher's encouragement helped him improve. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how practice helped Yousef improve.
I explained how Ms. Huda encouraged him.
I used at least two details from the story.
MID.modelAnswer: Ms. Huda encouraged Yousef by telling him that doing his best mattered more than winning, and she taught him to break long words into syllables. Yousef then built a daily routine of writing words down, saying them aloud, and using flashcards his sister made. Over several weeks, this practice helped his spelling improve and made him feel much more confident by the day of the bee.

keyWords.definition: the quality of continuing to try, even when something is difficult
keyWords.example: Her perseverance helped her finish the long race despite the pain.

keyWords.definition: a part of a word that contains one vowel sound
keyWords.example: The word elephant has three syllables.

keyWords.definition: something that is successfully accomplished through effort
keyWords.example: Finishing the marathon was a huge achievement for him.

keyWords.definition: the ability to recover quickly from difficulties and keep trying
keyWords.example: The team showed resilience after losing the first game of the season.

keyWords.definition: to say or pronounce something clearly
keyWords.example: The actor had to articulate every word so the audience could understand.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the story?
options: Winning a competition is the only true way to prove real effort
Spelling bees are unfair to students who are not naturally good at spelling from a young age
Yousef's sister deserves more credit than Yousef for his success
Consistent practice and encouragement helped Yousef grow more capable and confident
questions.why: The story emphasizes that Yousef's daily practice and his teacher's encouragement built his skill and confidence, even though he did not win.

wrong.A: Yousef's growth, not just winning, is shown as proof of his effort.
wrong.B: The story does not argue that spelling bees are unfair.
wrong.C: Yousef's sister helped him, but the story centers on Yousef's own effort and growth.

questions.stem: What specific technique helped Yousef manage unfamiliar, difficult words?
options: Dividing each word into smaller syllables to make it easier to pronounce
Memorizing the dictionary definition of every word on the list
Asking the judges for extra clues during each round of the competition
Avoiding words with more than two syllables in the contest
questions.why: Ms. Huda taught Yousef to break long words into syllables, which made them easier to remember and pronounce.

wrong.B: Memorizing dictionary definitions is not the technique described.
wrong.C: Asking judges for clues is not mentioned in the story.
wrong.D: Yousef practiced long words rather than avoiding them.

questions.stem: What was the most direct cause of Yousef's growing confidence in the weeks leading up to the bee?
options: Ms. Huda guaranteed that he would win the competition in the end
His consistent daily practice led to real, noticeable improvement
The other students decided not to compete in the bee that year
His sister took the test for him a few days beforehand
questions.why: Because Yousef practiced consistently, his spelling noticeably improved, which directly built his confidence.

wrong.A: Ms. Huda encouraged effort, not a guaranteed outcome.
wrong.C: There is no mention of other students withdrawing from the competition.
wrong.D: Yousef, not his sister, took the spelling tests.

questions.stem: What does Ms. Huda's advice about doing his best suggest about what she valued most as a teacher?
options: She valued trophies more than effort
She believed only naturally talented students deserved encouragement
She valued genuine effort and growth over simply winning
She believed practice was unnecessary for success
questions.why: By emphasizing effort over winning, Ms. Huda showed that she valued genuine growth more than trophies.

wrong.A: Ms. Huda's advice downplayed trophies in favor of effort.
wrong.B: Ms. Huda encouraged Yousef despite his early struggles, not only naturally talented students.
wrong.D: Ms. Huda gave Yousef techniques specifically to practice with.

questions.stem: Based on the sister's comment at the end, what does she seem to believe about the bee's past winners?
options: They never struggled with spelling in their lives, because spelling was easy for them
They were allowed extra practice time that Yousef did not get from the teacher
They did not actually deserve to win, and the judges made a mistake
They once struggled with spelling too, before persistent practice helped them improve
questions.why: Yousef's sister suggests that even past winners once struggled, and that persistent practice is what helped them improve.

wrong.A: The sister's comment suggests the opposite: that past winners did struggle.
wrong.B: There is no mention of unequal practice time.
wrong.C: The sister's comment does not question whether past winners deserved to win.

questions.stem: In the story, resilience most nearly means —
options: The ability to keep trying despite difficulty or setbacks
A formal reward given to the winner after a competition
A method for sounding out unfamiliar words in a book
A feeling of fear before speaking in public to a crowd
questions.why: Yousef's resilience was shown in his willingness to keep practicing even when spelling felt discouraging.

wrong.B: Resilience is not the same as a reward.
wrong.C: Sounding out words is related to syllables, not resilience itself.
wrong.D: Fear before speaking is nervousness, not resilience.

questions.stem: Which lists these events in the order they happened?
options: The bee begins, Yousef gets a low grade, Ms. Huda announces the competition
Yousef receives a low grade, the bee is announced, he practices, and the bee takes place
The bee takes place, Yousef builds a practice routine, Yousef receives a low grade
Ms. Huda announces the bee, the bee takes place, Yousef receives a low grade
questions.why: Yousef first receives a low grade, then the bee is announced, then he practices, and finally the bee takes place.

wrong.A: The bee happens last, not first.
wrong.C: Yousef builds his routine before the bee, not after.
wrong.D: Yousef receives his low grade before the bee is announced, not after it takes place.

questions.stem: Why does the author include Yousef's sister's comment at the very end of the story?
options: To suggest that Yousef should have simply asked the judges for help during the contest
To criticize the other students who won the spelling bee that year and their families
To reinforce the idea that effort and perseverance matter more than the final outcome
To explain exactly how all spelling bees are organized and judged in every school
questions.why: The sister's comment reminds Yousef, and the reader, that consistent effort matters more than where he placed in the competition.

wrong.A: The comment is not about asking judges for help.
wrong.B: The comment does not criticize the winners; it points out that they once struggled too.
wrong.D: The comment is about effort, not the rules of organizing a bee.

HIGH.prompt: The story suggests that effort and growth matter more than winning. Do you agree or disagree with this idea? Support your answer with evidence from the story.
checklist: I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that effort and growth matter more than winning. In the story, Yousef did not win the spelling bee, yet he spelled far more words correctly than he ever thought possible, which shows real growth from his earlier low grade. Someone might argue that only the winner truly succeeds, but Yousef's sister points out that even past winners once struggled, suggesting that persistence, not a single result, is what ultimately builds real skill.

LOW.stem: What did Ms. Huda give Yousef to help him?
options: A shiny gold prize
A brand new pencil
A big story book
A list of words
LOW.why: The text says she gave Yousef a list of words.

wrong.A: A prize is not mentioned.
wrong.B: A pencil is not mentioned.
wrong.C: A big book is not mentioned.

LOW.stem: The text says Yousef felt nervous. What does nervous mean?
options: happy and very proud
worried and a bit scared
sleepy and very tired
angry and very loud
LOW.why: Yousef was worried about spelling in front of others, so nervous means worried and a bit scared.

wrong.A: He felt proud later, not nervous.
wrong.C: Nervous is not sleepy.
wrong.D: Nervous is not angry.

LOW.stem: Why did Yousef's class clap at the spelling bee?
options: He spelled word after word.
He won first place at the bee.
He missed a very hard word.
He sang a song to the class.
LOW.why: His class clapped because he spelled word after word.

wrong.B: He did not win first place.
wrong.C: He missed a word later, and the class clapped before that.
wrong.D: Singing is not mentioned.

LOW.stem: Why did Ms. Huda say she was proud of Yousef?
options: He won the first prize at the bee
He never felt nervous at any time
He worked hard and did his best
He knew every word on the list
LOW.why: She said he worked so hard, and Yousef did his best even without winning.

wrong.A: He did not win first place.
wrong.B: Yousef's heart beat fast at the bee.
wrong.D: He missed one hard word.

MID.stem: Where did Yousef stand when he spelled the words at the bee?
options: At his own desk in the classroom
At the mic in front of the school
In the library next to Ms. Huda
In the yard with his sister
MID.why: He walked up to the mic in front of the whole school.

wrong.A: The bee was in front of the whole school.
wrong.C: The library is not mentioned.
wrong.D: His sister is not mentioned at the bee.

options: Small parts of a word
Long lists of tricky words
Rows of seats in a room
Quick tests given each day
MID.why: The text says to break each long word into smaller parts, called syllables.

wrong.B: The list of words is a different thing.
wrong.C: Seats are not mentioned.
wrong.D: The tests are not syllables.

MID.stem: Why was missing one hard word still a success for Yousef?
options: He got the highest grade in school
He was chosen to be the next teacher
He won a prize for the hardest word
He spelled more words than he expected
MID.why: The text says he spelled far more words correctly than he had ever imagined.

wrong.A: A grade is not mentioned there.
wrong.B: Being a teacher is not mentioned.
wrong.C: He did not win first place or a prize.

MID.stem: Why does the author begin by saying few things feel worse than struggling in front of your class?
options: To show that spelling is easy for everyone
To tell readers Ms. Huda was unkind
To show how hard spelling felt to Yousef
To explain why the bee was cancelled
MID.why: The opening helps readers understand how uncomfortable spelling made Yousef feel.

wrong.A: Spelling was hard for Yousef.
wrong.B: Ms. Huda encouraged him gently.
wrong.D: The bee was not cancelled.

HIGH.stem: In the story, what does the word "articulate" mean?
options: Write quickly on paper
Hide from other people
Say clearly and correctly
Count in a loud voice
HIGH.why: Dividing words into syllables made them easier to remember and say correctly.

wrong.A: Yousef was saying words, not only writing.
wrong.B: Hiding is not part of the meaning.
wrong.D: Counting is not mentioned.

HIGH.stem: What did Yousef do after taking his teacher's advice?
options: He quit the spelling contest
He set up a simple daily routine
He asked a friend to take his place
He practiced only on the weekend
HIGH.why: Yousef took her advice and set up a simple daily routine that he kept even on busy days.

wrong.A: He did not quit.
wrong.C: He did not ask anyone to replace him.
wrong.D: He practiced every day, not only on weekends.

HIGH.stem: Why did Yousef at first not want to take part in the bee?
options: He believed he had already won once
His sister told him not to join
He thought the words were too easy
He worried about embarrassing himself
HIGH.why: In the text, he worried that he would only embarrass himself in front of his classmates.

wrong.A: He had never felt confident about spelling.
wrong.B: His sister helped him later.
wrong.C: The words were tricky.

HIGH.stem: What does the phrase "one syllable at a time" suggest about Yousef's approach?
options: He tried to learn everything at once
He improved through small, steady steps
He copied all of his sister's answers
He skipped the harder words entirely
HIGH.why: He broke words into syllables and practiced a little at a time, so he improved in small steps.

wrong.A: One at a time is the opposite of everything at once.
wrong.C: His sister helped with flashcards, not answers.
wrong.D: He practiced a list of tricky words.
